title: Common Vulnerability Concepts: Injection and Unsafe Input Handling
learningObjectives: Explain the core ideas and terminology of common vulnerability concepts: injection and unsafe input handling.
Recognize the risks or mistakes this topic is intended to prevent.
Apply appropriate defensive practices in a beginner project.
Distinguish this topic from related security concepts and controls.
Review a simple design and justify improvements using evidence.

understand.concept: Injection occurs when data is unintentionally interpreted as instructions by another system or component. Unsafe input handling can cause unexpected behavior, data exposure, or integrity problems. Common prevention strategies include parameterized database queries, safe APIs, context-aware output encoding, allowlist validation, and avoiding dynamic execution of untrusted strings. This lesson focuses on recognition and prevention, not exploitation.
understand.whyItMatters: Treating input as data rather than executable instructions is a fundamental defensive habit.
understand.analogy: Think of a careful community space where entry, use of shared items, and privacy are guided by clear rules and appropriate checks.
understand.analogyLimit: Software security depends on technical boundaries, data flows, implementation details, and changing threats that this analogy cannot fully represent.

explain.narrative:
Injection occurs when data is unintentionally interpreted as instructions by another system or component. Unsafe input handling can cause unexpected behavior, data exposure, or integrity problems. Common prevention strategies include parameterized database queries, safe APIs, context-aware output encoding, allowlist validation, and avoiding dynamic execution of untrusted strings. This lesson focuses on recognition and prevention, not exploitation.

Apply these principles proportionately. Use established platform and library protections instead of improvising security-critical mechanisms. For a real application, confirm requirements and review the implementation with qualified peers.

examples.title: Prefer fixed choices
examples.explanation: Allowlisted options reduce unsafe dynamic behavior.

examples.title: Parameterized-query concept
examples.code:
const queryPlan = {template:'SELECT * FROM items WHERE id = ?',value:12};
console.log(queryPlan.template.includes('?'));
examples.explanation: A placeholder keeps values separate from SQL command text; use a database API that supports parameters.

examples.title: Encode output safely
examples.explanation: Output encoding must match the destination context; use platform helpers.

examples.title: Avoid dynamic evaluation
examples.code:
const safeApproach = 'parse data, do not evaluate untrusted strings';
console.log(safeApproach);
examples.expectedOutput: parse data, do not evaluate untrusted strings
examples.explanation: Dynamic code evaluation increases risk when data is untrusted.

commonMistakes: Assuming a feature is safe because it works in normal use.
Trusting client-side controls as the only enforcement.
Applying one generic transformation to every kind of input or output.
Exposing credentials or personal data in source, logs, or screenshots.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Given a fictional search form, identify where user input could be interpreted by a database or page renderer. Describe safe APIs and validation without attempting attacks.
steps: Given a fictional search form, identify where user input could be interpreted by a database or page renderer. Describe safe APIs and validation without attempting attacks.
Identify the relevant assets, inputs, or permissions.
Choose a control and explain why it applies.
Check edge cases and failure behavior.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Use a small fictional example. Never paste real credentials or private data.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Create a defensive design note for a search and comment feature. Cover database parameterization, output encoding, allowlists, input length limits, and tests for unusual values.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy project and no real secrets or personal data.
Create a defensive design note for a search and comment feature. Cover database parameterization, output encoding, allowlists, input length limits, and tests for unusual values.
Explain the decisions you made and limitations.
Identify at least one test or review step.

hints: Injection is about interpretation, not just unusual characters.
Keep query structure separate from user values.
Test edge cases safely in a local toy app.

questions.prompt: What is injection in this context?
options: Data is interpreted unexpectedly as instructions
questions.answer: Data is interpreted unexpectedly as instructions
questions.explanation: Injection results when data and instruction contexts are confused.

questions.prompt: How can database query injection be prevented?
options: Log the full query and credentials
questions.explanation: Parameters keep user values separate from query structure.

options: The correct encoding depends on where data is displayed
It removes the need for validation
It protects every possible context with one rule
questions.answer: The correct encoding depends on where data is displayed
questions.explanation: HTML, attributes, URLs, and other contexts require different handling.

questions.prompt: Why avoid evaluating untrusted strings as code?
options: It may turn data into executable behavior
questions.answer: It may turn data into executable behavior
questions.explanation: Dynamic evaluation can execute unintended instructions.

questions.prompt: Which is a defensive design choice?
options: Validate allowed values and use safe APIs
Use one sanitizer for every context
questions.answer: Validate allowed values and use safe APIs
